# Putting It All Together {#sec-ch18} It is the final semester. Elaf's analyses are spread over two years of scripts, written as she learned each method in this book. Her supervisor's advice for the last stretch is simple: "Before you write the results chapter, rebuild the whole thing, from the raw export to the last table, as one project that runs from start to finish. Then you will know that every number in your thesis is right, and you can answer any examiner's question by pointing to the code." This chapter does exactly that. It sets up a complete research project, runs Elaf's analysis from the messy survey export to the tables, figures, and sentences of a results chapter, and brings together the methods of the whole book. It then steps back: how to choose a method for a new question, the problems that every researcher meets, and where to go next. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## By the end of this chapter you will be able to - Organise a research project so that it runs from raw data to finished results. - Combine cleaning, description, modelling, and visualisation in one reproducible pipeline. - Report results in the style expected in a thesis, with numbers taken directly from the code. - Choose an appropriate method for a research question, using the map of this book. - Recognise common challenges in real research projects, and know where to learn more. ::: ## The shape of a research project Every quantitative project follows roughly the same path, and this book has followed it too (@fig-project). ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-project %%| fig-cap: "The path of a research project, with the chapters of this book that cover each step." flowchart LR A[Question and
design] --> B[Import
Ch 1–2] B --> C[Clean and
reshape
Ch 3] C --> D[Explore and
describe
Ch 4–5] D --> E[Test and
model
Ch 6–9] D --> F[Predict and
discover
Ch 10–15] E --> G[Report and
share
Ch 16–17] F --> G ``` The path is not a straight line in practice. Exploring the data sends you back to cleaning when you find a problem; a model's diagnostics send you back to exploring. What matters is that each step is written in code, so that going back and rerunning everything is easy. ### Organising the project A project that others (and your future self) can follow has a predictable structure. Elaf's final project looks like this: ``` wellbeing-thesis/ ├── wellbeing-thesis.Rproj the RStudio Project (Chapter 1) ├── README.txt what the project is and how to run it ├── data-raw/ │ └── wellbeing_raw.xlsx the survey export, never edited by hand ├── data/ clean data, created by the scripts ├── R/ │ ├── 01-clean-data.R raw export -> clean tables (Chapter 3) │ └── 02-analysis.R models and figures ├── output/ figures and tables, created by the scripts ├── results.qmd the results chapter (Chapter 16) ├── references.bib └── renv.lock package versions (Chapter 16) ``` The principles behind it: - **Raw data is read-only.** Everything in `data/` and `output/` can be deleted and recreated by running the scripts. - **Scripts are numbered** in the order they run, and each does one job. - **Paths are relative to the project**, using `here::here()` (Chapter 1), so the project runs on any computer. - **The README** says in a few lines what the project is and how to run it. The downloadable project for this chapter has the same structure, with working scripts (its `data/` and `output/` folders are created when the scripts run, and it has no `renv.lock`, which you create with `renv::init()` for your own project). The rest of the chapter walks through what the scripts do. ## From raw export to clean data The cleaning of Chapter 3, gathered into one script, runs in a few seconds. Here is its core, reading the raw export and producing the clean questionnaire and semester tables: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(stringr) library(readr) library(readxl) raw <- read_excel(data2thesis_example("wellbeing_raw.xlsx")) item_names <- c(paste0("stress_", 1:6), paste0("burnout_", 1:6), paste0("support_", 1:6), paste0("satisfaction_", 1:4)) responses <- raw |> filter(!str_detect(str_to_upper(`Q1_Student ID`), "^TEST")) |> select(-`Response ID`) |> distinct() |> rename(student_id = `Q1_Student ID`, workshop = `Workshop group`, considering_dropout = `Y1_Considered leaving?`) |> rename_with(~ item_names, .cols = Q11_1:Q11_22) |> mutate(across(all_of(item_names), ~ as.integer(na_if(.x, "99")))) questionnaire_clean <- responses |> select(student_id, all_of(item_names)) semesters_clean <- responses |> select(student_id, matches("_S[1-4]$")) |> pivot_longer(-student_id, names_to = c(".value", "semester"), names_sep = "_S") |> rename(gpa = GPA, sleep_hours = Sleep, study_hours = Study, exercise_days = Exercise, caffeine_mg = Caffeine, supervisor_meetings = Meetings, wellbeing = Wellbeing) |> mutate( semester = as.integer(semester), sleep_hours = parse_number(str_replace(sleep_hours, ",", ".")), across(c(gpa, study_hours, exercise_days, caffeine_mg, supervisor_meetings, wellbeing), parse_number), sleep_hours = if_else(sleep_hours > 24, NA, sleep_hours), study_hours = if_else(study_hours > 168, NA, study_hours), gpa = if_else(gpa > 4, NA, gpa) ) |> filter(!if_all(gpa:wellbeing, is.na)) ``` ::: Each step is explained in Chapter 3; the full script in the downloadable project also cleans the background variables. The most important line of any cleaning script is the check at the end. Does the result match the clean data? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} same <- function(mine, theirs) { mine <- as.data.frame(mine)[, names(mine)] theirs <- as.data.frame(theirs)[, names(mine)] isTRUE(all.equal(mine, theirs, check.attributes = FALSE)) } same(questionnaire_clean |> arrange(student_id), questionnaire |> arrange(student_id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} same(semesters_clean |> arrange(student_id, semester), semesters |> arrange(student_id, semester)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: Both are `TRUE`. In a real project there is no package to compare with, so the checks are the ones from Chapters 3 and 5: counts of categories, ranges of values, numbers of missing values, and a look at a few rows. From here on, the chapter uses the clean tables, together with the scale scores: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- questionnaire |> mutate( stress_4 = 6 - stress_4, stress = rowMeans(pick(stress_1:stress_6), na.rm = TRUE), burnout = rowMeans(pick(burnout_1:burnout_6), na.rm = TRUE), support = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE) ) |> select(student_id, stress, burnout, support) study <- students |> left_join(scores, join_by(student_id)) |> left_join(semesters |> filter(semester == 1), join_by(student_id)) ``` ::: `study` has one row per student, with background, questionnaire scores, and first-semester records, as in Chapter 7. ## Describing the sample Every results chapter begins by describing the participants, often in a table known as "Table 1". Elaf describes her sample by programme: ::: {#tbl-sample .cell tbl-cap='Characteristics of the sample, by programme.'} ```{.r .cell-code} mean_sd <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)) percent <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) describe <- function(d) { tibble( Characteristic = c("Students", "Age, mean (SD)", "Women", "Part-time", "Stress (1-5), mean (SD)", "Support (1-5), mean (SD)", "Wellbeing in semester 1, mean (SD)", "Considered dropping out"), Value = c(nrow(d), mean_sd(d$age), percent(d$gender == "Female"), percent(d$study_mode == "Part-time"), mean_sd(d$stress), mean_sd(d$support), mean_sd(d$wellbeing), percent(d$considering_dropout == "Yes")) ) } describe(filter(study, programme == "Master's")) |> rename(`Master's` = Value) |> left_join(describe(filter(study, programme == "PhD")) |> rename(PhD = Value), join_by(Characteristic)) |> left_join(describe(study) |> rename(All = Value), join_by(Characteristic)) |> knitr::kable(align = "lrrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Characteristic | Master's| PhD| All| |:----------------------------------|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:| |Students | 426| 174| 600| |Age, mean (SD) | 27.9 (3.3)| 34.2 (5.1)| 29.7 (4.8)| |Women | 52%| 53%| 52%| |Part-time | 26%| 39%| 30%| |Stress (1-5), mean (SD) | 3.2 (0.7)| 3.2 (0.7)| 3.2 (0.7)| |Support (1-5), mean (SD) | 3.2 (0.8)| 3.2 (0.7)| 3.2 (0.8)| |Wellbeing in semester 1, mean (SD) | 60.9 (12.1)| 59.3 (11.9)| 60.5 (12.0)| |Considered dropping out | 15%| 14%| 15%| ::: ::: Two small helper functions, `mean_sd()` and `percent()`, format the numbers the way theses report them, and `describe()` builds the column for any group of students, so the same code makes all three columns. Writing a small function whenever you would otherwise copy and paste code is one of the best habits to take from this book. (The **gtsummary** package produces such tables automatically, with many options, if you prefer.) ## Answering the research questions Here are three of Elaf's research questions, answered with the methods of Parts 2 and 3, each with a sentence written the way it will appear in her thesis. A small function formats p-values in the usual style: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} format_p <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < .001" else paste("p =", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p))) ``` ::: ### Did the workshop improve wellbeing, and did the effect last? (RQ3) Students were randomly invited to the wellbeing workshop after the first semester. The mixed-effects model of Chapter 9 uses all four semesters and every student: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(lme4) panel <- semesters |> left_join(students, join_by(student_id)) |> mutate(time = semester - 1) workshop_model <- lmer(wellbeing ~ factor(semester) * workshop + (time | student_id), data = panel) gaps <- expand.grid(semester = 1:4, workshop = c("Invited", "Not invited")) |> mutate(time = semester - 1) gaps$wellbeing <- predict(workshop_model, newdata = gaps, re.form = NA) gaps <- gaps |> pivot_wider(id_cols = semester, names_from = workshop, values_from = wellbeing) |> mutate(gap = Invited - `Not invited`) gaps ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 4 semester Invited `Not invited` gap 1 1 60.6 60.3 0.380 2 2 65.5 60.2 5.25 3 3 63.1 59.0 4.13 4 4 60.9 58.2 2.64 ``` ::: ::: > Wellbeing was similar in the two groups before the workshop (difference 0.4 points). After the workshop, invited students' wellbeing was 5.2 points higher in semester 2, but the difference narrowed to 4.1 points in semester 3 and 2.6 in semester 4. ### What explains students' GPA? (RQ5) The multiple regression of Chapter 7, with **broom**'s `tidy()` giving the coefficients and their confidence intervals as a data frame: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(broom) gpa_model <- lm(gpa ~ sleep_hours + study_hours + stress + support, data = study) gpa_table <- tidy(gpa_model, conf.int = TRUE) gpa_table |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 7 term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high 1 (Intercept) 2.14 0.145 14.7 0 1.85 2.42 2 sleep_hours 0.106 0.014 7.49 0 0.078 0.134 3 study_hours 0.007 0.001 6.27 0 0.005 0.009 4 stress -0.084 0.018 -4.68 0 -0.119 -0.049 5 support 0.111 0.017 6.63 0 0.078 0.144 ``` ::: ::: > Each additional hour of sleep was associated with a GPA 0.11 points higher (95% CI 0.08 to 0.13, p < .001), holding study hours, stress, and support constant. Together, the four predictors explained 25% of the variation in first-semester GPA (*n* = 587). ### Who considers dropping out? (RQ9) The logistic regression of Chapter 7, with odds ratios: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dropout_model <- glm( I(considering_dropout == "Yes") ~ stress + support + financial_worry + employment + study_mode, data = study, family = binomial ) dropout_table <- tidy(dropout_model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) dropout_table |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 7 × 7 term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high 1 (Intercept) 0.02 1.23 -3.26 0 0 0.19 2 stress 3.6 0.24 5.35 0 2.29 5.87 3 support 0.33 0.2 -5.44 0 0.22 0.49 4 financial_worry 1.57 0.12 3.73 0 1.25 2.01 5 employmentNone 0.55 0.44 -1.35 0.18 0.23 1.31 6 employmentPart-time j… 0.58 0.45 -1.19 0.23 0.24 1.41 7 study_modePart-time 1.32 0.37 0.75 0.45 0.63 2.68 ``` ::: ::: `I()` lets a condition be used directly as the outcome, and `exponentiate = TRUE` turns the log-odds into odds ratios and their confidence intervals. > Each one-point increase in stress (on the 1–5 scale) was associated with 3.6 times the odds of considering dropping out (95% CI 2.3 to 5.9), and each one-point increase in supervisor support with 0.33 times the odds (95% CI 0.22 to 0.49). Chapters 10 to 14 went further with this question, asking how well dropout can be *predicted*; the thesis reports that logistic regression predicted as well as any machine learning model (cross-validated AUC about 0.80), which is itself a finding worth stating. ## One figure for the thesis A thesis figure often combines panels. The **patchwork** package joins ggplot2 plots with `+` (side by side) and `/` (one above the other), and `plot_annotation()` labels the panels: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) library(patchwork) panel_a <- gaps |> pivot_longer(c(Invited, `Not invited`), names_to = "workshop", values_to = "wellbeing") |> ggplot(aes(x = semester, y = wellbeing, colour = workshop)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.8) + labs(x = "Semester", y = "Predicted wellbeing (0-100)", colour = "Workshop") panel_b <- ggplot(study, aes(x = sleep_hours, y = gpa)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#1f6f8b") + labs(x = "Sleep (hours a night)", y = "GPA (semester 1)") (panel_a + panel_b) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") & theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![(A) Predicted wellbeing by semester and workshop group, from the mixed-effects model. (B) First-semester GPA against hours of sleep, with a regression line.](18-putting-it-together_files/figure-html/fig-thesis-1.png){#fig-thesis fig-alt='Two panels. Panel A: two lines over semesters 1 to 4; the invited group rises above the not-invited group in semester 2, and the gap narrows afterwards. Panel B: a scatter plot of GPA against sleep hours with an upward-sloping regression line.' width=864} ::: ::: `&` applies the theme to both panels. `ggsave()` saves the figure at the size and resolution a thesis or journal requires (Chapter 4): ```r ggsave(here::here("output", "figure-1.png"), width = 18, height = 8, units = "cm", dpi = 300) ``` ## The results chapter The final step is the one Chapter 16 prepared: the tables, figures, and sentences above go into a Quarto document, `results.qmd`, in which every number is written with inline code. The downloadable project contains such a document, built from this chapter. When the data changes, or an examiner asks for a different model, Elaf changes the code and renders again, and the whole chapter is updated. ## Choosing a method A new research question starts with two questions about the data: what kind of **outcome** is it, and how are the **observations** related? @fig-choose summarises the methods of this book as a guide. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-choose %%| fig-cap: "A guide to choosing a method, with the chapters that cover each." flowchart TD Q{What is the goal?} -->|Describe| D[Summaries and plots
Ch 4–5] Q -->|Explain or compare| O{Outcome type?} Q -->|Predict new cases| P[Machine learning
Ch 10–14] Q -->|Find groups or
structure| U[PCA, factor analysis,
clustering
Ch 8, 13] Q -->|Forecast over time| T[Time series
Ch 15] O -->|Numeric| N{Repeated or
nested data?} O -->|Yes / No| L[Chi-square, logistic
regression
Ch 6–7] N -->|No| R[t-test, ANOVA,
regression
Ch 6–7] N -->|Yes| M[Mixed-effects
models
Ch 9] ``` @tbl-map shows how each of Elaf's research questions was answered. | Research question | Method | Chapters | |---|---|---| | RQ1 What does graduate life look like? | Plots, descriptive statistics | 4, 5 | | RQ2 Do students sleep less than 7 hours? | One-sample t-test, confidence interval | 6 | | RQ3 Does the workshop improve wellbeing? | Two-sample t-test; mixed-effects model | 6, 9 | | RQ4 Do faculties and study modes differ? | ANOVA, post-hoc tests | 6, 7 | | RQ5 What explains GPA? | Multiple regression | 7, 12 | | RQ6 Does the questionnaire measure what it should? | Factor analysis, Cronbach's alpha | 8 | | RQ7 Are there student profiles? | Cluster analysis, mixture models | 8, 13 | | RQ8 How do wellbeing and GPA change? | Mixed-effects models | 9 | | RQ9 Who considers dropping out? | Logistic regression; classification | 7, 10, 11, 14 | | RQ10 Can final GPA be predicted? | Regularised regression, boosting | 12 | | RQ11 What challenges do students describe? | Text coding with a language model | 17 | | RQ12 How many counselling visits next year? | Time series forecasting | 15 | : Elaf's research questions and the methods used to answer them {#tbl-map} ## Challenges every researcher meets Real projects rarely go as planned. Some problems are almost universal, and the book has met most of them: - **Messy data.** Every real dataset needs cleaning, and cleaning takes longer than analysis. Do it in code, check after every step, and keep the raw file untouched (Chapter 3). - **Missing data.** Ask *why* data is missing before deciding what to do; dropping incomplete cases can bias results when the missing data is not random, as with the students who left Elaf's programme (Chapter 5). - **Small samples.** Small samples give wide confidence intervals and low power, and make complex models overfit. Report effect sizes with intervals, keep models simple, and plan the sample size before collecting data (Chapters 6 and 12). - **Many tests.** The more tests you run, the more false alarms. Decide your main analyses in advance, correct for multiple comparisons where needed, and report exploratory results as exploratory (Chapters 6, 7, and 16). - **Assumptions.** Check them with plots rather than with tests alone, and know the alternatives: robust tests, non-parametric tests, transformations, and mixed models (Chapters 6, 7, and 9). - **Correlation and causation.** Observational data rarely proves causes. Think about confounders, such as sleep behind the caffeine effect, and use randomised designs where you can, as Elaf's workshop did (Chapters 5 and 7). - **Prediction versus explanation.** A model that predicts well may explain little, and the reverse (Chapter 10). - **Communicating with others.** Supervisors, co-authors, and examiners may use other software. A clear results chapter with tables, figures, and an appendix of code serves them all; export data with `write_csv()` or `haven::write_sav()` when they need it (Chapter 2). ## Where to go next This book is a beginning. Depending on your field, the next methods to learn may be: | Topic | What it is for | Packages | |---|---|---| | Structural equation modelling | Confirmatory factor analysis, path models, latent variables | lavaan | | Bayesian statistics | Models with prior knowledge and full uncertainty | brms, rstanarm | | Survival analysis | Time until an event, such as dropping out | survival | | Meta-analysis | Combining results from several studies | metafor | | Text analysis | Words, sentiment, and topics in documents | tidytext, quanteda | | Spatial data | Maps and geographic data | sf | | Publication tables | Automatic, formatted tables of results | gtsummary, modelsummary | | Interpreting models | Predictions and effects from any model | marginaleffects | : Topics for further study {#tbl-next} Some of the best resources are free online: *R for Data Science* [@wickham2023] for data skills, *Regression and Other Stories* [@gelman2020] for regression, *An Introduction to Statistical Learning* [@james2021islr] and *Tidy Modeling with R* [@kuhn2022] for machine learning, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice* [@hyndman2021] for time series, and *Mastering Shiny* [@wickham2021shiny] for dashboards. Appendix E lists more, including courses and videos in Arabic. You do not have to learn alone. The R community is known for being welcoming to beginners: the Posit Community forum and Stack Overflow answer questions; **R-Ladies** and local R user groups run meetings around the world; **TidyTuesday** publishes a new dataset every week for people to practise on and share their plots; and *R Weekly* collects news and tutorials. Asking a clear question, with a small reproducible example, is itself a skill, and the same skill that makes an AI assistant useful (Chapter 17). ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## In your field: nutrition science The same path works for any dataset, in a few lines. R's `ToothGrowth` data comes from an experiment on the growth of teeth in 60 guinea pigs given vitamin C at three doses, as orange juice (`OJ`) or as a vitamin C supplement (`VC`). A complete mini-project, from data to a reported result: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tooth <- ToothGrowth |> mutate(dose = factor(dose)) tooth |> summarise(mean = mean(len), sd = sd(len), n = n(), .by = c(supp, dose)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` supp dose mean sd n 1 VC 0.5 7.98 2.746634 10 2 VC 1 16.77 2.515309 10 3 VC 2 26.14 4.797731 10 4 OJ 0.5 13.23 4.459709 10 5 OJ 1 22.70 3.910953 10 6 OJ 2 26.06 2.655058 10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tooth_model <- aov(len ~ supp * dose, data = tooth) summary(tooth_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) supp 1 205.4 205.4 15.572 0.000231 *** dose 2 2426.4 1213.2 92.000 < 2e-16 *** supp:dose 2 108.3 54.2 4.107 0.021860 * Residuals 54 712.1 13.2 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: The two-way ANOVA of Chapter 7 shows that tooth length depends on the dose, the form of vitamin C, and their combination: orange juice helps more than the supplement at low doses, but not at the highest. The same steps (prepare, describe, model, report) would take a few more lines with a plot and a Quarto report. Whatever your field, the path from data to thesis is the one this book has followed. ::: ## Chapter review ### Summary - A research project follows a path from question and design through import, cleaning, exploration, and modelling to reporting and sharing, often going back to earlier steps. Writing every step in code makes going back easy. - Organise projects with read-only raw data, numbered scripts, relative paths, a README, and a Quarto results document; everything else can be recreated. - Check the cleaned data at the end of the cleaning script, then describe the sample, answer each research question with the method suited to it, and report results with numbers taken directly from the code. - Small helper functions (for formatting means, percentages, and p-values) avoid copying and pasting code; broom turns model results into data frames; patchwork combines plots. - Choose methods by the goal (describe, explain, predict, find structure, forecast), the type of outcome, and how the observations are related. - Messy and missing data, small samples, many tests, assumptions, and causation are challenges in every project; the chapters of this book give tools for each. ### Key terms Research workflow, project structure, raw data, pipeline, sample description ("Table 1"), helper function, broom, patchwork, reporting sentence, method choice. ## Exercises The [playground](../playground/chapter18.html) has these and more, and the downloadable project contains Elaf's complete project. 1. Download the Chapter 18 project, run `R/01-clean-data.R` and `R/02-analysis.R`, and render `results.qmd`. Then change one cleaning rule (for example, treat ages above 70 as impossible) and render again. Which numbers change? 2. Add a row to the sample table (@tbl-sample) for the share of students with children. 3. Write a reporting sentence, with inline numbers, for the effect of support on GPA in the regression model. 4. Add a third panel to the thesis figure: wellbeing by faculty as a box plot. 5. Choose a research question from your own field. Using @fig-choose, decide which method you would use, and which chapter of this book you would reread first. ## Further reading - *R for Data Science* [@wickham2023] covers the whole workflow of this chapter in more depth, and is the natural next book for most readers. - *Regression and Other Stories* [@gelman2020] is an excellent guide to building, checking, and reporting regression models in real research.
